name: Erik Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at ten to five, and I'm in the parlour by half past with the radio on. We milk eighty cows in a herringbone parlour that was old when I took the tenancy on, twenty-two years ago, on the county council farm estate. After breakfast it's feeding, scraping out, checking feet, and this time of year the barley ground is ploughed so it's mostly the cows and the silage clamp. Tariq does the evening milking four days a week, and we eat our sandwiches together on the feed bin at noon and argue about football.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cows, honestly. You know every one of them, which one kicks, which one waits at the back. What wears me out is the paperwork and the milk price, which the dairy sets and we just take. My knees aren't what they were either, and Ingrid says I limp up the stairs like her grandad did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably at the union branch meeting in the back room of the Plough. Every few years somebody comes round selling the future, and most of it ends up rusting behind a shed. I'd say the cows still need milking and the people still need paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, plain and simple. I'm fifty-eight, I've got maybe seven years left in me, and I don't want to spend them learning a computer. If nothing changes, I get to finish the way I started: two hands, one old parlour and Tariq on the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd renew the tenancy at the next review in 2028, keep putting a bit by each month, and maybe replace the vacuum pump in the parlour, which is on its last legs. That's a few thousand, and we've got it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a weather forecast that says the storm's going round us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a lot of these things end up rusting behind a shed. Is there one you're thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The automatic heat-detection collars. A salesman talked half the valley into them about ten years back, and two winters later the batteries died and nobody bought new ones. Mine are still in a feed sack in the workshop. I never even put them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone on the farm be worse off in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Tariq keeps his hours, the vet keeps coming, the dairy keeps squeezing us like they always have. That's not AI, that's just the dairy.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads at the union branch that I told them so. Every few years someone sells us the future and most of it ends up rusting behind a shed.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, plain and simple. I've got maybe seven years left in me and I don't want to spend them learning a computer, so I get to finish the way I started.
S0.do: Keeps going exactly as now. Plans to renew the council tenancy at the 2028 review, keeps saving each month and replaces the worn parlour vacuum pump for a few thousand.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit smug. The storm goes round him.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I get to finish the way I started: two hands, one old parlour and Tariq on the evenings.
S0.fieldNote: Erik's default is suspicion of anything sold as the future, and he has a sack of unused heat-detection collars to prove his point. He measures his remaining working life in years, about seven, and wants them to look like the last twenty-two. The real squeeze he names is the milk price, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks, Erik. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same old story: the big farms get the kit first and the small ones pay for it. I'd bring it up at the union branch and say we need rules on who owns all that data the dairy collects off us. I might even write to the farming paper, which I've done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the dairy starts telling us how to farm. They already send a man round with a tablet. If they start paying a better price only to farms with robot milkers, that's me pushed out by a contract clause, not by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking the way I do and dig my heels in for as long as the price lets me. I'd go to every union meeting about it and push for a fair-price deal for herds that don't automate. If the milk contract changes, I'd ask Ingrid to go through it with me line by line, because she reads those things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a pebble in my boot. I can still walk, but I notice it every step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned robot milkers. Has anyone near you put them in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petersen, two farms down, put in two robot units three years ago. His cows queue up at three in the morning like it's a cash machine, and he told me he sleeps better. I said to him, Petersen, you sleep better, but your phone wakes you every time a cow sneezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tariq in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I don't like. Tariq's thirty-four, two little girls, and the evening milking is half his income. If I ever did go robot, he's the first one who loses out, and I wouldn't do that to him while I've got a say.

S1.say: It's the same old story: the big farms get the kit first and the small ones pay for it. We need rules on who owns the data the dairy collects off us.
S1.think: The real threat is the dairy contract, not the machine. If they pay a better price only to robot farms, I'm pushed out by a contract clause.
S1.do: Keeps milking by hand and attends every union meeting, pushing for a fair-price deal for herds that don't automate. Asks his partner Ingrid to read any new milk contract with him line by line.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a pebble in his boot. He can carry on, but notices it constantly.
S1.quote: I said to him, Petersen, you sleep better, but your phone wakes you every time a cow sneezes.
S1.fieldNote: Erik frames everything through power: who owns the data, who writes the contract. His loyalty to Tariq, his relief milker, is a big reason he won't automate. He's resistant, but not passive; he'd organise through the union rather than change his own farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd be angry. I'd say the government let a handful of tech firms take over farming without a vote, and that somebody needs to slam the brakes on. I'd be the one standing up at the branch meeting asking why the union isn't outside Parliament.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it frightens me. Two years is nothing on a farm. The tenancy review is in 2028, the same year, and the council could decide a robot dairy pays more rent than a tired man with bad knees. Twenty-two years on that land, and I could lose it in one committee meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ring the union and the tenants' association and get everyone on the council estate in one room, because there are fourteen of us. I'd write to our councillor and our MP the same week. Then I'd talk to Ingrid about bringing retirement forward to sixty and living off the savings and the rent from the cottage, because I won't learn to run a robot dairy at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake at two working out what I'd say to the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Mira, she's a nurse in the city, and I'd ask her if the hospital's buying robots too. Jonas is an electrician, and he'd probably say, Dad, someone's got to wire them. He'd be right, and I'd still hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra money you've saved change how this feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we won't go hungry, I know that. We've got the savings and the cottage in town that we rent out. But money doesn't keep the cows, and it doesn't stop me feeling like I've been sent home early.

S2.say: The government let a handful of tech firms take over farming without a vote, and somebody needs to slam the brakes on. Why isn't the union outside Parliament?
S2.think: It frightens me, because my tenancy review is in 2028, the same year. The council could decide a robot dairy pays more rent than a tired man with bad knees.
S2.do: Calls the union and gathers the fourteen council-estate tenants in one room within the first week. Writes to his councillor and MP, and plans with Ingrid to retire at sixty on savings and cottage rent.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, rehearsing what he'd say to the council at two in the morning.
S2.quote: Twenty-two years on that land, and I could lose it in one committee meeting.
S2.fieldNote: The 2028 tenancy review turns an abstract scenario into a very specific date for Erik. His savings protect his income but not his place on the land, and that's what scares him. He moves straight to collective action and politics, and he talks about early retirement as being 'sent home early'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's slow it down a little. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say much the same as the fast one, just with less shouting. Five years is enough for the union to get organised, so I'd push them to draw up what fair rules for robots on farms look like before the firms write their own. I'd say workers like Tariq need a guarantee of something, retraining or a payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I probably get to see the tenancy through one more review, in 2028, before the robots really arrive. Five years is about the same as my knees have got left, so maybe the robots and I retire together. That's a joke, but only half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd renew the tenancy in 2028 but for the shortest term the council offers. I'd stop putting money into the parlour and put it in savings instead, about four hundred a month extra. And I'd plan to sell the herd around sixty-two and hand the tenancy back while there's still someone who wants it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could plan. It's like knowing the bank's coming in five years instead of next Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop spending on the parlour. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means patching instead of fixing. The vacuum pump gets a rebuild, not a new one. The cracked yard concrete stays cracked. You run it down, gently, like an old dog you're not going to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most, if not yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tariq, again, and the young ones on the estate. There's a couple, Lena and Sam, took a council farm two years ago with forty goats and a loan. Five years gives me a soft landing. It gives them a cliff.

S3.say: The union should draw up fair rules for robots on farms before the firms write their own. Workers like Tariq need a guarantee of something, retraining or a payout.
S3.think: I probably get to see the tenancy through one more review before the robots really arrive. Five years is about what my knees have left, so maybe we retire together.
S3.do: Renews the tenancy in 2028 for the shortest term on offer and saves about four hundred a month extra instead of spending on the parlour. Plans to sell the herd around sixty-two.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like knowing the bank comes in five years instead of next Tuesday.
S3.quote: Five years is about the same as my knees have got left, so maybe the robots and I retire together.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up almost exactly with Erik's own working life, which takes much of the fear out. He shifts from protest to quiet wind-down, running the parlour down 'like an old dog'. His concern moves outward to younger tenants who have loans and no runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say this is a job for the young ones and the union, not for me. I'd still say the government needs rules on who owns the robots and the land. But I'd say it calmer, like a man reading the paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2036 I'm sixty-eight and I'll be out of it, watching from a bench. It's Jonas and Mira's generation that needs to worry. For me it's mostly about whether the farm goes to another family or to a company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned and retire at sixty-five, like I always meant to. I'd stay active in the union and push for the council to keep its farms for new young tenants, not lease them to robot companies. I might put a bit more into savings, but nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of sadness. Like watching the swallows go in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to see happen in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the council to promise in writing that the estate stays for families. A council farm is supposed to be a ladder for young people, not a shelf for somebody's machines. That's worth ten years of meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said retire at sixty, sixty-two and sixty-five across these pictures. Which is it really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, you caught me. Sixty-five if I'm left alone, earlier if I'm pushed. The money's there either way, so it's really about pride, not need.

S4.say: This is a job for the young ones and the union, not for me. The government still needs rules on who owns the robots and the land.
S4.think: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and out of it, so it's Jonas and Mira's generation that needs to worry. For me it's whether the farm goes to a family or a company.
S4.do: Keeps going and retires at sixty-five as planned. Stays active in the union, campaigning for the council to keep its farms for young tenants rather than lease them to robot firms.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a quiet sadness, like watching the swallows leave in September.
S4.quote: A council farm is supposed to be a ladder for young people, not a shelf for somebody's machines.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Erik stop fighting for himself and fight for the estate. When I named his shifting retirement ages, he admitted the money is there and it's about pride. The difference between this and the two-year picture is almost entirely the tenancy timing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because it lands on the same year as my tenancy review. What would help is the council promising sitting tenants first refusal and a fair notice period, and a proper fund for farm workers like Tariq, paid for by whoever sells the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about the farmer and the robot. Nobody asks if the cows mind. Mine know my voice, and I'd like to think that's worth something, even if nobody's going to pay for it.

headlineQuote: Mine know my voice, and I'd like to think that's worth something, even if nobody's going to pay for it.
portrait: Erik Farah is a 58-year-old dairy farmer who has milked eighty cows on a council-owned tenancy for twenty-two years, in a parlour as tired as his knees. He's left-leaning, a loyal union member and deeply suspicious of anything sold as the future. He's comfortable financially, with savings and a rented-out cottage, but his place on the land depends on a council tenancy review in 2028. That date drives his reactions: the two-year AGI picture alarms him, while five or ten years lets him plan a quiet wind-down and turn his energy to protecting younger tenants and his relief milker, Tariq.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would arrive in the same year as his council tenancy review and the council might prefer a robot dairy.
whatWouldHelp: First refusal and fair notice for sitting council tenants, and a fund for farm workers like Tariq paid for by the companies selling the robots.
